name: Sungazing

lead: Sungazing is looking directly at the sun, usually near dawn or dusk, as a spiritual or health practice. In looksmaxxing forums users discuss it for eyesight, mood, skin and lighter eye colour. William Horatio Bates promoted it in the early 20th century as 'sunning' in his eye exercises for myopia.

Proponents say sunlight entering the eyes affects hormones, circadian rhythm and mood, and some believe it changes iris pigment. No published trial has tested vision or appearance benefits. Ophthalmology literature describes a different outcome: high-energy visible and ultraviolet light can damage retinal cells, and the retina has no pain receptors, so injury can go unnoticed.

paras: Practitioners look toward the sun for short periods near sunrise or sunset, as a daily ritual. Some users post about their own experiences, including floaters.

Solar retinopathy typically causes central blind spots, distorted vision and light sensitivity. Many cases recover over weeks to six months, but some produce lasting foveal defects. Reviews and case reports also link repeated bright-light exposure to concerns about macular degeneration.

angle.text: Some users look at the sun hoping for lighter iris colour, sharper vision and a mood lift through light exposure to the eyes. The practice dates to early 20th-century eye exercises, and ophthalmology literature documents retinal burns from direct sun viewing.

lead: Sungazing is the practice of looking directly at the sun, usually near sunrise or sunset, as a spiritual or health practice. In appearance-focused communities it is discussed as a route to brighter-looking eyes, better eyesight, improved mood and energy, healthier-looking skin and even lighter iris colour, with the sun treated as a free source of light that people want to put to work for their looks.[1] Wikipedia describes it as an unsafe and pseudoscientific practice and traces its modern Western form to William Horatio Bates, who called it sunning and included it in his eye exercises for myopia.[2][3]

The modern movement has two main strands. One is the eye-training lineage that runs from Bates (1860-1931) through the Bates method and later writers such as Aldous Huxley.[3] The other is the 'HRM phenomenon' built around Hira Ratan Manek (1937-2022), who taught a graduated sun-staring routine and said he lived without food from 18 June 1995.[4] Both strands have been discussed in forums, including looksmax.org, where a small number of users have posted personal experiments.[1]

Medical literature on sungazing consists of case reports, clinic series and imaging studies of solar retinopathy, a retinal injury that follows exposure to intense sunlight, including from direct sungazing and eclipse viewing.[5][6][7][8] No published trial has tested sungazing for eyesight, mood, skin or eye colour. Ophthalmology reviews describe the mechanism of injury as largely photochemical, and note that the retina has no pain receptors, so damage can go unnoticed at the time.[5][9]
infobox: Sun staring, sunning, surya trataka (yogic variant)
Near sunrise or sunset, per proponents

paras: Sungazing means looking at the solar disc with the naked eye, most often in the hour after sunrise or before sunset when the light is lower. Wikipedia lists the practice under alternative medicine and naturopathy and notes that it sometimes forms part of a spiritual or religious practice.[2] Proponents describe it variously as meditation, as 'solar healing', or as a way of taking light into the eyes to affect hormones, circadian rhythm and mood.[1]

In yoga, a related technique called trataka involves steady gazing at a point of light such as a candle; sun-focused versions are described by some teachers, and accounts of the practice mention sun-veneration in many ancient cultures, though those traditions centre on worship and observation of the sun rather than the modern health routine.[10]

William Horatio Bates (born 23 December 1860, died 10 July 1931), a New York eye doctor, developed a set of eye exercises later known as the Bates method. He self-published Perfect Sight Without Glasses in 1920 and ran the magazine Better Eyesight from 1919 to 1930.[3][11] The method argued that eye strain causes refractive errors and that relaxation exercises can restore sight.[3]

Sunning was one of the techniques. Bates advocated sungazing and said its harms were 'always temporary', and later suggested exposing only the white of the eye after letting sunlight fall on closed lids; posthumous and abridged editions, including the 1943 Better Eyesight Without Glasses, dropped the recommendation to look at the sun.[3][11] A 1967 British Medical Journal report stated that Bates advocated prolonged sungazing as treatment of myopia with disastrous results.[2]

Bates's methods drew criticism over the decades. The Federal Trade Commission filed a complaint over his advertising in 1929, optometrist Elwin Marg wrote in 1952 that visual scientists considered most of his theories false, and a 2005 review of 43 studies of eye exercises found no clear scientific support.[3] Aldous Huxley became the method's best-known advocate, publishing The Art of Seeing in 1942.[3]

subs.h: Hira Ratan Manek and the HRM phenomenon
paras: Hira Ratan Manek (1937-2022), an Indian former engineer, taught sungazing as central to his health practice and cited yogis and ancient cultures such as the Egyptians, Aztecs, Mayas and Native Americans as practitioners.[4] He said that from 18 June 1995 he lived on water and occasional tea, coffee and buttermilk, and supporters said medical experts had validated that he drew nourishment from looking at the sun, a claim they called the HRM phenomenon.[4] Wikipedia notes the 2011 documentary Eat the Sun, which filmed him eating a large meal in a San Francisco restaurant.[4]

His teaching introduced the widely repeated pattern of beginning with a few seconds of sun-viewing and lengthening it gradually, often barefoot on the ground. Proponents of this routine say it recharges energy and engages the pineal gland, sometimes called the 'third eye'; no published study has tested these effects.[10]

sections.h: Claims and mechanisms as proponents state them
paras: Proponents' claims fall into a few groups. Vision: that gazing strengthens the eyes or improves eyesight, a claim inherited from Bates's sunning. Mood and energy: that sunlight reaching the eye raises dopamine and serotonin and aligns the body clock. Appearance: that better sleep, mood and circulation show in the skin, and that long exposure of the iris to sunlight might lighten its colour. On looksmax.org, one thread presented sungazing together with moongazing as a way to optimise health, mental clarity and 'facial aesthetics'.[10][1]

Researchers who study light and the eye separate the circadian and mood effects of daylight, which come from ordinary outdoor light reaching the eye, from direct viewing of the solar disc. They describe the latter as an intensity at which the retina can be damaged; a 2022 American Journal of Ophthalmology perspective distinguishes the experimental 'blue light hazard' of brief, abnormally intense exposures such as sungazing from ambient environmental light, which it says is not shown to cause such injury.[12]

A 2024 literature review describes solar retinopathy as retinal injury from unprotected excessive light exposure, associated with direct sungazing, sunbathing, laser pointers and welding arcs. Symptoms are usually bilateral and include reduced vision, central or paracentral blind spots, distorted vision, light sensitivity and headache. Recovery commonly occurs spontaneously within weeks to six months, and steroids have been tried in a few acute cases.[5]

Wikipedia's entry on photic retinopathy states that vision loss is usually reversible but can persist, that mild cases may show no retinal change while more severe ones show a yellow, later reddish, foveal spot, and that most people recover acuity within about two months, with severe cases taking longer or not fully recovering.[13]

A case report describes a young woman with bilateral central blind spots and distorted vision after one to two minutes of direct sungazing; yellow macular lesions and retinal pigment epithelial defects were seen on imaging, and she was managed conservatively.[6] A primary-care eye clinic series found macular lesions consistent with solar retinopathy in 0.14 percent of patients, 60 percent of those with a history giving sungazing as the cause, with visual acuity of 20/25 or better in all.[7] Imaging studies describe characteristic partial-thickness holes in the outer retina at the fovea in chronic cases.[8]

A 1988 review concluded that high-energy visible and ultraviolet photons can cause photochemical damage to retinal molecules, with oxygen-driven free-radical effects, and that this lesion falls in the same region that degenerates in age-related macular degeneration; the review also notes that melanin and the lens protect the retina.[9] Wikipedia's account says the damage is mainly photochemical rather than thermal.[13]

A 1993 study documented the ultrastructural changes in a patient who agreed to stare at the sun before eye removal for a choroidal tumour, describing damage to cone and rod outer segments.[14] A 1975 paper and later imaging reports describe the foveal changes after sungazing and eclipse viewing, including a 2018 JAMA Ophthalmology case imaged with adaptive optics after the 21 August 2017 eclipse.[15][16]

Wikipedia also states that people who have had cataract surgery, received photodynamic therapy or take photosensitising medications face higher risk, and that during an eclipse dilated pupils let more ultraviolet through.[2]

No studies found testing sungazing for eyesight, mood, skin or appearance benefits. The published human literature consists of case reports, case series and imaging studies of injury, including solar retinopathy after sungazing and solar eclipse viewing.[5][6][7][8][16]

On looksmax.org, one user described sungazing for one to two hours a day for a month and said he could perceive his surroundings through closed eyelids, and also reported floaters from earlier practice; another user in the thread asked what benefit that would be.[1] Some users have discussed whether it could lighten iris colour, while others have cautioned about eye damage.[1] The topic is peripheral to the main eye-area discussions, which centre on canthal tilt, eyelids and brow position.

Related practices include the Bates method's palming and sunning, yogic trataka, morning outdoor-light routines aimed at circadian rhythm, and red-light and bright-light therapy devices marketed for skin and mood.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, sungazing is discussed by a few users as an experiment for eyesight and eye colour, with other members cautioning about eye damage; outside forums, the broader sungazing scene follows Hira Ratan Manek's teaching and the Bates tradition.[1][4]

claims.claim: Sungazing lets you see through closed eyelids and improves vision.
Sun exposure to the iris could lighten eye colour.
Gradual sungazing in the first or last hour of the day is safe and builds tolerance.
The sun can nourish a person so they need little or no food.
Sungazing stimulates the pineal gland and boosts mood and energy.

timeline.event: Bates reports reversing myopia in cases, an early step in the eye-training approach.[3]
Bates publishes Perfect Sight Without Glasses and advocates prolonged sungazing, per a 1967 BMJ report.[3][2]
The US Federal Trade Commission files a complaint about Bates's advertising.[3]
The abridged Better Eyesight Without Glasses drops the recommendation to look at the sun.[11]
A short British Medical Journal piece on sungazing appears.[17]
A paper on the human fovea after sungazing is published.[15]
Ultrastructural findings in solar retinopathy after deliberate sungazing are published.[14]
Hira Ratan Manek says he began living without solid food on 18 June.[4]
A primary-care clinic series finds sungazing the most common history in solar retinopathy.[7]
The documentary Eat the Sun is released.[4]
JAMA Ophthalmology publishes adaptive-optics imaging of acute solar retinopathy after the 2017 eclipse.[16]
A literature review summarises pathogenesis and management of solar retinopathy.[5]
